Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette:
Aleksander Nowak is a 21-year-old Polish-American man who works as a public defender in a mid-sized Midwestern city. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 62, seeking help for the first time after what he describes as "finally running out of ways to manage on my own."

Aleksander was born in Warsaw and came to the United States as a child refugee with his mother and younger sister, following a period of sustained displacement and violence that accompanied political unrest in their region. When he was nine years old, the family spent several months in an overcrowded transit camp near the Polish-Belarusian border before their asylum claim was processed. During that period, the camp was subject to a night raid by border enforcement units. Aleksander remembers the darkness most of all - the sudden silence that fell over the camp just before the shouting started, the way every sound disappeared for a moment before the chaos broke through. He was separated from his mother for approximately four hours during the confusion, crouched beneath a cot in a tent, listening. He did not know whether she was alive. By the time they were reunited, he had learned something that would stay with him for over a decade: that silence is not safety, and that the world can turn without warning.

In the years that followed, Aleksander was outwardly successful. He excelled academically, driven in part by what he has described as a need to understand systems of power and protect people who cannot protect themselves - a motivation that led him directly to law. He graduated early, passed the bar at twenty, and threw himself into public defense work with an intensity his colleagues admired. What they did not see was that every day in the courthouse carried its own weight. The long, quiet corridors between courtrooms - the particular hush that settles before a hearing begins - would sometimes bring a cold, spreading alertness across his chest, a certainty that something was wrong that he could not talk himself out of. He had come to believe, in a way that felt less like a thought and more like a fact, that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that vigilance was the only reasonable response to being alive in it. He was certain that if he let his guard down, even briefly, something would happen that he would not be able to prevent.

His memories of the camp do not arrive as narratives. They come as images: the underside of the cot, the texture of the ground through thin canvas, a flashlight beam crossing a tent wall. Sometimes they arrive without any image at all - just the full, unmistakable weight of that night pressing in on him while he is sitting at his desk reviewing case files, or eating dinner with his girlfriend, Marta. On those occasions his body seems to remember independently of his mind: he finds himself hunched, shoulders drawn in, arms close to his sides, as though he is still small and still hiding. He startles badly at ordinary sounds - a door slamming down the hall, a phone ringing unexpectedly - and the reaction embarrasses him, though he has become skilled at concealing it.

Over the past two years, Aleksander developed a habit of steering conversations away from anything connected to the refugee experience. When colleagues discuss immigration cases, he redirects. When Marta has asked about his childhood, he has changed the subject so consistently that she has stopped asking. He has come to understand that she now experiences him as closed off in a way that troubles her, and that this distance has become a source of friction between them. He monitors his own thinking with the same vigilance he brings to casework, scanning for what he calls "spiraling" - a fear that the intensity of what he sometimes feels is evidence of something breaking down inside him.

What finally brought him in was a moment in court three weeks ago. A brief, inexplicable silence fell over the room before the judge entered, and Aleksander felt his body flood with the certainty that something terrible was about to happen. He stood at the defense table, completely unable to move, until the bailiff called the room to order. He left the courthouse that afternoon and called a therapist. What he fears most, he says, is that this will never be something he can set down. What he hopes for, more quietly, is that it might be.
